rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all eight compounds and identify critical pairs while limiting the time penalty. The intermediate temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.
Only the first pair needs improvement, and all peaks already elute before 10 minutes. Raise temperature to test selectivity for that pair while keeping the gradient unchanged.
A modestly shallower gradient should improve the first pair from R = 1.41 toward full resolution. Retain 60 C, which improved selectivity, with ample room before the 10-minute time penalty.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; now test a shorter fully resolved method. This gradient slope lies between injections 2 and 3, so it should preserve R above 1.5 while shortening the last-peak time.

Shift the gradient window upward while keeping its slope close to injection 4 to test whether initial low-organic time can be removed. Monitor the first pair for loss of resolution as the peaks elute earlier.

Restore the low starting organic fraction needed by the first pair and test a slope just steeper than injection 4. The lower endpoint should retain full elution with only a short final hold, potentially shortening the fastest fully resolved run.
Probe the unexplored low-temperature selectivity regime to see whether the first pair separates in the opposite elution order. Injection 6 remains the fastest fully resolved method found so far.

Test whether a small temperature increase separates the late cluster seen at 25 C while preserving the improved early-pair selectivity. Shortening the gradient also probes a faster alternative to the 60 C methods.

Test a faster, shifted gradient at 25 C, where the early pair had substantial resolution margin. Changing the starting fraction and slope may break the late three-peak coincidence while shortening retention.

Test an intermediate temperature to separate the late cluster without approaching the early-pair coelution seen at 40 C. The shallower gradient should support resolution, while the higher starting fraction limits retention time.

Return to the favorable 60 C selectivity and reduce the slope relative to injection 5. This tests whether a shallower gradient can restore full early-pair resolution with the higher starting organic fraction.

Test whether a further increase in starting organic fraction, compensated by a shallower gradient, can preserve early-pair resolution. This extends the window-trimming comparison while keeping a sufficiently strong endpoint for complete elution.

Test whether a higher starting fraction improves early-pair selectivity at 35 C while shortening the run relative to injection 10. The slightly shallower slope should help preserve separation of the later cluster.

Probe the resolution boundary with a gradient slightly steeper than injection 6, keeping the favorable low starting fraction. This may shorten the last-peak time while retaining full credit for the first pair.
Refine the higher-starting-fraction method with a slope between injections 5 and 11. This tests whether the first pair can remain fully resolved while shortening retention relative to injection 11.

The fastest fully resolved method is near the first-pair resolution limit. Test a shallower gradient for a more robust maximum-score alternative, aiming to increase the minimum resolution while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.
Shorten injection 16 by one gradient-time step to balance the first-pair and third-pair resolution margins. This should retain the maximum CRF while reducing the last-peak time relative to that run.

Use a slope between injections 16 and 17 to balance the two limiting pairs near R = 2. Trimming the endpoint should keep all peaks inside the gradient and retain maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Return near the fastest fully resolved method with a slightly shallower slope than injection 6 and a higher endpoint to avoid hold-phase elution. This should retain maximum CRF with a small additional resolution margin and a last-peak time near 7 minutes.

Test a compromise between speed and resolution margin using a higher starting fraction and a shallower slope than injection 11. This should strengthen the first-pair separation while keeping all peaks comfortably below 10 minutes.

Reduce the endpoint from injection 19 to improve the limiting first-pair resolution while retaining an eight-minute gradient. The last peak should remain near the gradient endpoint and below 10 minutes, preserving maximum CRF.

Increase the endpoint one step from injection 21 to shorten retention while preserving a useful first-pair resolution margin. Its slope matches the successful injection 3, so full resolution is expected with a shorter programmed gradient.

Shorten injection 22's programmed gradient while preserving its slope and expected early-pair resolution. Test whether the final hold at 0.50 still elutes the last peak before 10 minutes without sacrificing maximum CRF.

Refine between injections 11 and 15 with a slope of 0.070 organic fraction per minute. This should preserve full first-pair resolution with slightly more margin than injection 15 while shortening retention relative to injection 11.

Use the final injection to test a fully gradient-eluted alternative with a slope between injections 21 and 22, targeting full resolution with additional margin below 10 minutes. Injection 6 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method.
